name: fig1_decomposition
title: How much of NCAP cities' reported fall in PM2.5 survives weather and network correction, and how did their satellite PM2.5 move relative to comparison cities?
question: How much of a city's reported improvement is real?
caption: (a) Mean change in annual ground PM2.5 from 2018 to 2025 over the 18 NCAP cities with a station valid every year (16 of them with only one such station), decomposed in the proposal's order. Reported change (all stations as reported, after the audit's cleaning) -23.6%; removing the part the deweathering model does not reproduce (+0.8 pp removed), modelled weather (+2.9 pp removed) and the change in which stations exist (+5.8 pp removed) leaves a weather- and composition-corrected change of -14.1% (balanced panel, deweathered). Bars: GAM (primary); squares: LightGBM; intervals: 95% cluster bootstrap over cities. H4 (reported fall minus corrected fall) = +9.5 pp (95% CI +4.8 to +14.5). (b) Satellite PM2.5 of the listed units relative to their synthetic comparison units after listing: the 18 cities' units pooled (Phase 7, Layer A restricted) +3.8% (95% CI +1.0 to +6.6), and the shrunken city-level relative change of each illustrative city (Phase 8; 95% credible interval): Chennai +1.4% (-2.9 to +5.4); Hyderabad +5.3% (+1.5 to +9.0); Kolkata +1.6% (-2.7 to +5.7); New Delhi -1.3% (-5.2 to +3.0). This is a different quantity on a different time base from (a), so it is drawn on its own axis and not subtracted. Each removed part is labelled with the step it makes, so its sign is the direction of its bar. (c) The same decomposition for Chennai, Hyderabad, Kolkata, New Delhi, chosen by a rule on station counts that was written after viewing the per-city results (DEC-191); every city is in Figure S3. Intervals are station bootstraps where a city has more than one station in a stratum, otherwise none can be estimated and the GAM–LightGBM gap shows the model uncertainty. H1 is not identified by this design (registered pre-trend test failed): not an effect of NCAP.
alt: Waterfall chart. Across 18 NCAP cities, the reported fall in ground PM2.5 from 2018 to 2025 averages -23.6%; after removing modelled weather and the change in which monitors exist it is -14.1%, so about 40% of the reported fall does not survive correction. The largest part removed is network composition (+5.8 pp removed). Four illustrative cities (Chennai, Hyderabad, Kolkata, New Delhi) show the same steps; in 1 of them the correction turns a reported fall into a rise. On a separate axis, the same cities' satellite PM2.5 rose 3.8% relative to comparison units after listing. That relative change is not identified as an effect of NCAP.
